ca_top_rope_wall.blurb: A small granite wall tucked into the Horse Flats climbing zone of the Angeles National Forest, up Angeles Crest Highway and reached on foot from the campground. Of its 16 lines, most are top-rope or short trad, with a handful of boulder problems, one sport route and one aid line. The free climbs bunch up around 5.7 to 5.8, with a second cluster near 5.11 and a few 5.10 and 5.12 lines; the boulder problems run from V3 up to V6. It suits a low-key day of top-roping close to camp rather than a big-mileage outing, and tends to feel secluded.

ca_morbid_mound.blurb: A low, isolated mound rising from the desert floor north of the Indian Cove camping loops in Joshua Tree National Park. The walls are only about 20 to 30 feet high and the stone is coarse and crumbly, so this is a place for easy practice rather than quality climbing. Of its 16 routes, 14 are trad and two are top-rope. Many are very easy, a group sit around 5.7 to 5.9, and a few reach 5.10 and 5.11. Large top-rope groups and beginners use it often, and it makes a handy spot to practise building anchors close to the road.

ca_lizard_s_hangout.blurb: A modest, plain-looking formation in the Hidden Valley part of Joshua Tree National Park, just northwest of the Roadside Rocks and close to the road. Its 16 climbs are mostly short trad cracks, with three easy boulder problems at V0. Free routes range from very easy through 5.7 to 5.9 (the biggest group), with a few at 5.10 and 5.11. Because the pitches are brief, many parties set up top-ropes instead of leading. The routes sit on the southwest side, so walk around from the road side to reach them. A convenient stop for moderate crack practice.

ca_oj_buttress.blurb: A newer wall in Pine Creek Canyon above Bishop, sitting between two neighbors, Crack of Noon Buttress on one side and the G.O.T. Crag. Mostly bolted sport lines (12 of 16) with a few trad routes, and the emphasis is moderate: roughly 5.8 to 5.12, with 5.10 the biggest group and a handful at 5.11. The longer lines need a 70 m rope. The wall goes into shade during summer afternoons, which makes it a reasonable pick when the canyon is hot. Expect a talus-and-dirt-road approach of about 15 to 20 minutes with an orange roof as the landmark.
ca_oj_buttress.parking_note: Use the small dirt turnout on the Pine Creek Road shoulder a short way beyond the Pratt's Crack turn-off.
ca_oj_buttress.approach: Follow dirt paths and an old roadbed up from the road, then work up the talus slope toward the orange-roofed section of the wall.

ca_dear_john_buttress.blurb: One of the closest and most popular buttresses at Lover's Leap near Highway 50 east of Lake Tahoe, set on the west side of the main cliff. Mostly trad (14 of 16 routes) on steep to slightly overhanging rock about 130 feet tall, with one or two pitches each and plenty of flared cracks. Grades start at 5.8 and are heavy in the 5.11 range, with a few at 5.10 and 5.12 and one 5.13. The east-facing wall is shaded by trees most of the day, so it stays cool in hot weather, though weekends in summer can be busy.
